problem: LLM-based robot navigation relies on API calls to large models (privacy, latency, network dependence), while small language models (SLMs) that can run on edge devices reason poorly and produce unreliable output formats; generic compression methods (quantization, distillation, pruning) are slow, compute-hungry and weak on specific tasks.
motivation: Edge deployment gives fast response, privacy and network autonomy, so robots need local SLMs that plan multi-goal navigation from language. The authors observe that domain fine-tuning fixes output format and map knowledge, and that a strong teacher LLM can further correct the student through prompting and feedback.
key_idea: Boost sub-3B SLMs for language-based multi-point navigation by LoRA fine-tuning on a human-in-the-loop generated dataset, followed by a teacher-student iteration where GPT-4 acts as prompt engineer and feedback receiver, then execute the output waypoints with Nav2.
insight: Ablations show fine-tuning alone beats iteration alone (it fixes JSON output format and internalizes map info), and iteration on top of fine-tuning adds a further 30-40% SR. Because the map is baked into the weights, the prompt can omit it, cutting inference time (2.87 s vs 15-224 s for GPT-4 pipelines). Un-tuned SLMs get 0% on PDDL/STL-style pipelines, showing output-format constraint is critical.
method: LoRA fine-tuning: PEFT/LoRA adapts SLMs (tau-0.5B, TinyLlama-1.1B, danube-1.8B, openllama-3B, mm4-3B) to output JSON with 'explanation' and 'positions' (list of x,y coordinates) given task text and map landmarks.

Human-in-the-loop dataset generation: an LLM generates tasks from hand-written examples plus environment info; humans score them; the scored tasks are fed back to the LLM over several cycles to produce ~1400 hospital-sim tasks (1:3:2:1 for 1/2/3/4+ goals).

Teacher-student iteration: GPT-4 teacher generates prompts for the fine-tuned student from the task, map info and feedback from previous results; success/failure of each result updates the feedback; iterated for several rounds. The teacher is removed at deployment.
Navigation controller: the ordered goal list from the SLM is passed to ROS Navigation2, which drives the robot to the points sequentially.
Edge deployment: the system runs on Jetson Orin NX 16GB on a DIABLO wheel-legged robot.

setting.backbone: Small LMs <3B (openllama-3B, tau-0.5B, TinyLlama-1.1B, danube-1.8B, mm4-3B), LoRA fine-tuned; GPT-4 as teacher during iteration only
setting.training_data: ~1400 synthetic LLM-generated, human-scored navigation tasks in a hospital sim (~100 test tasks); ~100 tasks per real environment for fine-tuning
setting.observation: Text task description plus map landmark coordinates and attributes (no vision)
setting.action_space: Ordered list of target 2D coordinates executed by Nav2 (waypoint-level)
setting.simulator: Gazebo-style hospital world with TurtleBot3 Waffle (simulator not named); plus real world
setting.privileged: Pre-built map with landmark coordinates given as input/baked in via fine-tuning; GT goals used for teacher feedback during iteration

numbers.eval_set_note: ~100 designed test tasks (tables report 30 tasks worth of SR granularity)
numbers.extra: fine-tuned on ~1400 tasks; teacher removed at test; memory 8 GB

numbers_note: Custom benchmark, not a standard one. Real-robot results and ablations/accuracy curves are given only in figures, so not extracted.
results: With FASTNav, openllama-3B reaches 70% SR and tau-0.5B 63.33% SR, versus 6.67-36.67% for GPTQ/Int4/distilled compression baselines (at least ~30% better). openllama-3B with FASTNav (70% SR, 2.87 s) beats GPT-4 AutoTAMP (53.33%) and LLM-as-planner (46.67%) and is close to GPT-4 LLM+P (76.67%, 15.38 s).
limitations: Needs a lot of task-specific fine-tuning data and per-environment fine-tuning and iteration.
Small evaluation (~30-100 tasks in sim, 10 in real), custom benchmark, not comparable to standard VLN benchmarks.
